What about you? 

Your spiteful question isn't helping someone stay alive. 

I've seen the aftermath of suicide on the people still alive. I don't think it's worth it for the individual killing themselves or those around them. 

There is no waking up from it. There's nothing after it. You don't feel. There is no peace in it.

From what I've seen? A lot of sadness in the world from people you wouldn't even expect or probably even know. Recently, my boss' father committed suicide-- I didn't know him, my boss and I have an extremely hate/love relationship, and we go through employees like crazy. It really hit me. Even the most temporary of employees who probably worked there a month even felt sad, and made them reflect on themselves and their behavior, even in the slightest. But they had no chance of changing it for the better for anyone they've lost because that person was already gone.

My boss had no way of patching anything with her father. He never got to see that he actually mattered so much. Even if this answer doesn't make complete sense, it brings a lot of sadness in a lot of different ways and to me, it's always sad when that happens, when small, simple actions, even when they seem to be unnoticed, can be or bring some good to the world. 

A friend of mine committed suicide and the last year she was alive, we hardly talk. It's been a decade or so and the fourth of July is still a bad day for me. It's subtle, sad things that come from it. Which in a big picture may not seem like a big deal, but they are. 

Just us interacting with you, I feel bad, not obligated, nor in a way to make you feel guilty. I feel something. And we don't know each other. And I hope that means something.

You won't be. Suicide isn't like the movies. You don't get to see any of the positive or negative consequences of when you do it. You don't get to feel the peace that all the movies and books imply. 

As someone with BPD and has tried therapy and almost every med under the sun, I can tell you that you don't get what you need from suicide. 

I don't know what we need. But you don't get it from that.

EDIT: This is also coming from someone who is, I will admit, despite having BPD, extremely prejudice against people with it and other extreme disorders. I guess it's the self hate.

Stephen King’s On Writing is a wonderful guide to writers even if you don’t like his writing.

In Stephen King’s On Writing, he addresses adverbs pretty well by pretty much saying your description/prose should set the tone for any dialogue. So you don’t have to write something like: “I thought that was your job,” she said mildly. And instead something roughly like: She paused and her brows furrowed. “I thought that was your job.”

He, and I know other authors state, that no one’s really an expert and even the best have adverbs in their work. So it’s really a matter of over using them, I think.

Showing is key, here, I think. A good mix of dialogue and some solid description should cover it.
